Storebrand dates its history to 1767, when a scheme for fire insurance of buildings in Norwegian towns was set up. The name comes from a fire insurer for goods and movable property founded in Christiania in 1847. The most dramatic period came after the merger with UNI Forsikring in 1991. The following year UNI Storebrand failed in its attempt to build a Nordic insurance group around Sweden's Skandia, the holding company was placed under public administration, and only after a refinancing in 1993 did the shares return to the stock exchange.

Today Storebrand is above all a pension and savings group in Norway and Sweden, with its head office at Lysaker. The Swedish pension company SPP was bought from Handelsbanken in 2007, and in 2022 Danica Pensjon in Norway and the savings app Kron were added. Asset management includes the SKAGEN and Delphi funds, the private equity firm Cubera and Denmark's AIP, which manages infrastructure and renewable energy funds. Alongside this, the group runs non-life and personal insurance and a bank for retail customers. Folketrygdfondet, the Norwegian state's fund manager, is the largest shareholder.

For the dividend, the guaranteed pensions are the most important thing to understand. These are older pension contracts with an interest rate guarantee, a portfolio in run-off that shrinks as the obligations expire. While they remain, they tie up a lot of capital, and Storebrand plans to pay out what they release, mainly through buybacks of its own shares. Under the policy the ordinary dividend is to be kept at least at the same amount in kroner as the year before, as long as solvency is good enough, and at an even higher solvency the board intends to propose an extra dividend or buybacks. At its capital markets day in December 2025 the group set out an ambition for double-digit annual dividend growth up to and including 2028.

SUBC.tekst:
Subsea 7 lays pipelines, cables and subsea equipment on the seabed and ties fields back to platforms, production vessels or shore. The company was formed in 2011, when Acergy and Subsea 7 Inc. merged. It is registered in Luxembourg and has its head office in London, while the shares trade in Oslo. One part of the business develops oil and gas fields, in 2026 among other places on the Norwegian continental shelf, in Brazil, in the US and off Côte d'Ivoire. The other, Seaway7, installs foundations and cables for offshore wind farms and in 2026 has worked mostly in British and French waters. Both use a fleet of specialist vessels that the company owns itself. Subsea 7 also holds a smaller stake in SLB OneSubsea, which makes subsea equipment.

For a shareholder, the merger with Italy's Saipem is what matters most. The agreement was signed in July 2025 and approved by shareholders in September the same year, and the companies expect to complete it in the second half of 2026. For each Subsea 7 share, owners receive 6.688 shares in the combined Saipem7, which will have its head office in Milan and trade both there and in Oslo. Just before the merger takes effect, Subsea 7 will pay an extraordinary dividend. Siem Industries, the company of chairman Kristian Siem, is the largest owner today and will also be a major owner in Saipem7.

Until the merger, the company's own contracts carry the dividend. Projects run over several years, and the order book covers much of next year's work too, so one weak quarter says little on its own. The dividend is declared in kroner, but the amount is calculated from a sum in dollars, and the company hedges the currency in advance. Once the merger is completed, the board of Saipem7 decides what shareholders receive.

TEL.tekst:
Telenor was founded as Telegrafverket in 1855, was called Televerket from 1969 and took the name Telenor in 1995. The company was listed on Oslo Børs in December 2000, and the state is still the largest owner through the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Fisheries. In Norway, Telenor is the largest player in both mobile and broadband. The company describes itself as the only telecom operator with significant operations in all four Nordic countries, with Telenor in Norway, Sweden and Denmark and DNA in Finland. In July 2026 Telenor agreed to buy a controlling stake in the Swedish broadband provider Bahnhof.

The Asian business has shrunk quickly. Telenor Pakistan was sold at the turn of 2025/2026, and in January 2026 Telenor agreed to sell its stake in Thailand's True Corporation. What remains is the majority in Grameenphone in Bangladesh and a minority stake in CelcomDigi in Malaysia. The past in the region still follows the company: in September 2026 Telenor ASA was charged in a case about its former business in Myanmar.

The dividend for a financial year is declared as one amount and split in two, with one part paid in June and one in October. The policy is that the ordinary dividend per share shall rise from year to year, and in recent years the increases have been small. Telenor also buys back its own shares. In the programme from May 2026 a proportional share of the state's shares is redeemed, so that the state's stake stays the same, and the shares are cancelled afterwards. The company itself calls 2026 a transition year, with parallel IT systems and restructuring costs that are planned to decline towards the end of the year and through 2027.

VAR.tekst:
Vår Energi traces its roots back to the very first production licence on the Norwegian continental shelf, awarded in 1965, and to Eni Norge, which was founded the same year. Today's company was formed in 2018, when Eni Norge merged with Point Resources. Since then it has grown through acquisitions: ExxonMobil's stakes in fields operated by others came in 2019, and Neptune Energy's Norwegian business in 2024. Vår Energi was listed in February 2022, and Italy's Eni is still the largest owner with a clear majority of the shares.

The company holds stakes in many of the producing fields on the Norwegian shelf. It is itself operator of Balder, Ringhorne, Gjøa and Duva in the North Sea, Fenja in the Norwegian Sea and Goliat in the Barents Sea. A large part of the gas is sold to Europe. This breadth means a production stop at one field matters less for the whole than at a producer with few fields, but everything still lies on one shelf and under one tax regime.

The dividend is set as a total dollar amount for the whole company each quarter. It is converted to kroner per share at Norges Bank's dollar rate when the dividend is announced. The long-term policy ties the payout to a share of cash flow from operations after tax, viewed over a full cycle. In July 2026 Vår Energi and BlueNord agreed to merge, and BlueNord's shareholders are to receive new shares in Vår Energi and cash. This gives Vår Energi production outside Norway for the first time, from Tyra and the other hubs in the Danish North Sea. The company has said the merger will increase its capacity to pay out, but the dividend will also be shared among more shares than before.

VEI.tekst:
In 2020 Veidekke sold its property development business, which had grown up over several decades alongside its contracting operations. The sale gave shareholders a large dividend and the company a solid financial position, and since then Veidekke has been a pure contractor in Norway, Sweden and Denmark. The company was founded in 1936 and is today divided into building and infrastructure in Norway and in Sweden, while the Danish business is run under the name Hoffmann.

The infrastructure arm is the most varied. It builds and maintains roads, railways, airports, power plants and water and sewage facilities, and it has its own asphalt plants, supplies aggregates and runs landfills. In Norway Veidekke has road maintenance contracts across the whole country, and in northern Sweden it supplies the mining industry. The company describes its Norwegian building arm as the country's largest building contractor, and it builds homes, offices, shopping centres, schools and healthcare buildings. Veidekke calls its way of working interaction, with customers and suppliers involved from an early stage.

The shareholder register is dominated by long-term Norwegian owners. The housing cooperative OBOS is the largest shareholder and Folketrygdfondet, which manages the Norwegian state's domestic pension fund, the second largest, and the employees together own a significant stake through discounted share programmes and through Stiftelsen Veidekkeansattes Aksjekjøp. The dividend policy sets a floor at a large share of annual profit, and in the years up to 2025 almost all of the profit went to shareholders. What can put pressure on the dividend is loss-making projects, and the acquisitions the company is now making in order to grow, as when the asphalt contractor Nord Vei og Asfalt in Troms was bought for cash in 2026.

VEND.tekst:
Vend Marketplaces is the listed company that remained when Schibsted split up. The media houses were spun off in 2024, the company changed its name from Schibsted Marketplaces to Vend in 2025, and that autumn the A and B shares were merged into a single share class with one vote per share. Since then the share has traded under the ticker VEND. The foundation Stiftelsen Tinius is still the largest shareholder.

What remains is digital marketplaces in the Nordic countries, divided into mobility, real estate, jobs and recommerce. The well-known brands are FINN in Norway, Blocket in Sweden, DBA and Bilbasen in Denmark, and Tori and Oikotie in Finland. In real estate FINN is the clear market leader in Norway. Most revenue comes from listings paid for by car dealers, estate agents and employers, and it follows activity in the housing, car and labour markets. A growing share comes from transactions, as when a private individual sells a car to a dealer through Nettbil or lets a home through Qasa. Alongside its operations, Vend owns a minority stake in the marketplace group Adevinta.

The dividend policy is an ordinary dividend that is to rise gradually over time and is decided once a year. Free cash flow after dividends and investments is also returned to shareholders as share buybacks or extraordinary dividends, and buybacks have made up a large part of this. When Adevinta sold its Spanish business in 2026, Vend said its share of the proceeds paid out would be passed on to shareholders, mainly as buybacks. The dividend alone therefore shows only part of what the company returns.

WAWI.tekst:
Wallenius Wilhelmsen took its current form in 2017. That year Sweden's Wallenius and Norway's Wilhelmsen combined the stakes they had held together in the shipping companies EUKOR and ARC and in the logistics company Wallenius Wilhelmsen Logistics, a partnership that went back to 1999. Wilh. Wilhelmsen Holding, itself listed, is the largest owner. Wallenius Lines, owned by the Swedish Soya Group, is the other large shareholder. The head office is in Oslo.

The ships carry cars, construction machinery and other rolling cargo on scheduled routes between continents, and the logistics arm takes over on land with terminals, vehicle preparation and onward transport to dealers. Much of the volume is on multi-year contracts with car and machinery makers, and renewals are announced to the stock exchange at regular intervals. One customer relationship is closer than the others: Hyundai Motor Group owns a minority stake in the Korean subsidiary EUKOR and has a freight agreement with it that runs until 2029. The company is building new ships that can run on LNG, and in October 2026 it raised new equity to expand the newbuilding programme. Wilhelmsen subscribed for its share, while Wallenius stayed out.

The dividend comes twice a year and is set in dollars but paid in kroner. For the first half of 2026 it was calculated as half of underlying profit, with an extraordinary addition on top. How much is left for shareholders therefore depends both on the freight market out of Asia and on how much capital the newbuildings tie up in the years ahead.

WWI.tekst:
Wilh. Wilhelmsen Holding was founded in Norway in 1861 and is today a maritime holding company with three parts. Maritime Services sells chemicals, gases, ropes, welding equipment and refrigerants to the merchant fleet, acts as ship agent in ports, and handles technical management and crewing of ships for other owners. Its customers are shipping companies and cargo owners all over the world. New Energy consists mostly of NorSea, which runs supply bases for the offshore industry in Norway, Denmark and the United Kingdom. It also holds the stake in Edda Wind, which owns service vessels for offshore wind. Wilhelmsen took Edda Wind off the stock exchange in 2025 together with two other large owners.

Measured by the balance sheet, it is the third part, the strategic holdings, that weighs most. One is a large stake in the car carrier Wallenius Wilhelmsen, the other a holding in South Korea's Hyundai Glovis. Both provide logistics for the car industry. The Glovis shares used to sit in the listed company Treasure, but in 2025 Wilhelmsen bought out the remaining shareholders and took Treasure off the exchange. In October 2026 Wilhelmsen committed to subscribe for its share of a private placement in Wallenius Wilhelmsen.

Thomas Wilhelmsen is chief executive and controls the company through Tallyman AS, which holds a majority of the votes. This ticker is the A share, which carries voting rights at the general meeting. The aim is a steady annual dividend split into two payments, one in spring and one in autumn, and the second is decided by the board under an authorisation from the general meeting. Share buybacks are used as well. Much of the cash coming into the parent company is dividends from Wallenius Wilhelmsen, so what happens in the car carrier market is felt here too.

YAR.tekst:
Yara traces its beginnings to 1905, the year Sam Eyde and Kristian Birkeland founded Norsk Hydro. The fertiliser business was separated from Hydro and listed as a company of its own in 2004, and the Norwegian state is still the largest owner. Yara makes mineral fertiliser, mostly nitrogen-based, and sells it to farmers in much of the world. The company also sells ammonia and industrial chemicals. Ammonia is made from natural gas, so the gas price feeds straight into costs.

The plants in Europe pay the European gas price, and Yara wants to spread that risk. The strategy is to source more of its ammonia from the US, where gas is priced off Henry Hub. In June 2026 Yara withdrew from buying the ammonia plants at Louisiana Clean Energy Complex because the return did not meet the company's requirements. A few days later Yara agreed to buy Gulf Coast Ammonia in Texas City, a new plant that is still ramping up. The set-up resembles the one Yara already has in Freeport, Texas. The plant faces a damages claim over a terminated purchase agreement, which the plant company rejects with Yara's support.

Under the dividend policy, the ordinary dividend is to be half of net income, as long as debt stays within the targets the company has set and the credit rating remains at mid investment grade. Cash dividends are the main route, with share buybacks on top. In the weak years of 2023 and 2024 the dividend was well above half of earnings. For 2025 earnings rose sharply, and the dividend the board proposed in February 2026 was announced as an ordinary dividend, not an extraordinary one. The investments in the US are planned to stay within the normal level of capital expenditure, so the dividend policy can remain unchanged while they are under way.
